title: No. 56 — The Same Subject Continued (The Total Number of the House of Representatives) (Madison)
paragraphs: The second charge against the House of Representatives is that it will be too small to possess due knowledge of the interests of its constituents.

Since this objection clearly proceeds from comparing the proposed number of representatives with the great extent of the United States, the number of inhabitants, and the diversity of their interests — without taking into account the circumstances that will distinguish the Congress from other legislative bodies — the best answer is a brief explanation of these peculiarities.

It is a sound and important principle that the representative ought to be acquainted with the interests and circumstances of his constituents. But this principle can extend no further than to those circumstances and interests to which the authority and care of the representative relate. Ignorance of various minute and particular objects that do not lie within the compass of legislation is consistent with every attribute necessary to a proper performance of the legislative trust. In determining the extent of information required for exercising a particular authority, recourse must be had to the objects within the scope of that authority.
What are to be the objects of federal legislation? Those most important, and which seem most to require local knowledge, are commerce, taxation, and the militia.

A proper regulation of commerce requires much information, as has been remarked elsewhere. But as far as this information relates to the laws and local situation of each individual State, a very few representatives would be quite sufficient vehicles to convey it to the federal councils.

Taxation will consist, in great measure, of duties involved in the regulation of commerce. So far the preceding remark applies to this object. As far as it may consist of internal collections, more diffuse knowledge of the State's circumstances may be necessary. But will not this also be possessed in sufficient degree by a very few intelligent men, broadly elected within the State? Divide the largest State into ten or twelve districts, and there will be no peculiar local interests in any that will not be within the knowledge of the district's representative. Besides this source of information, the laws of the State, framed by representatives from every part of it, will themselves be almost a sufficient guide. In every State, regulations on this subject have been made and must continue to be made, which will in many cases leave little more for the federal legislature to do than to review the different laws and reduce them into one general act. A skillful individual in his study, with all the local codes before him, might compile a law on some subjects of taxation for the whole Union, without any aid from oral information. It may be expected that whenever internal taxes may be necessary, and particularly in cases requiring uniformity throughout the States, the more simple objects will be preferred. To be fully sensible of the ease this will give to this branch of federal legislation by the assistance of the State codes, we need only suppose for a moment that this or any other State were divided into a number of parts, each having and exercising within itself a power of local legislation. Is it not evident that a degree of local information and preparatory labor would be found in the several volumes of their proceedings, which would very much shorten the labors of the general legislature, and render a much smaller number of members sufficient for it? The federal councils will derive great advantage from another circumstance. The representatives of each State will not only bring with them a considerable knowledge of its laws, and a local knowledge of their respective districts, but will probably in all cases have been members, and may even at the very time be members, of the State legislature, where all the local information and interests of the State are assembled. From there it may easily be conveyed by a very few hands into the legislature of the United States.

(The observations made on the subject of taxation apply with greater force to the case of the militia. For however different the rules of discipline may be in different States, they are the same throughout each particular State. They depend on circumstances that can differ but little in different parts of the same State.)

(With regard to the regulation of the militia, there are scarcely any circumstances about which local knowledge can be said to be necessary. The general face of the country, whether mountainous or level, most fit for operations of infantry or cavalry, is almost the only consideration of this nature that can occur. The art of war teaches general principles of organization, movement, and discipline, which apply universally.)

The attentive reader will see that the reasoning used here, to prove the sufficiency of a moderate number of representatives, in no respect contradicts what was urged on another occasion regarding the extensive information that representatives ought to possess and the time that might be necessary for acquiring it. This information, so far as it may relate to local objects, is rendered necessary and difficult, not by a difference of laws and local circumstances within a single State, but by those among different States. Taking each State by itself, its laws are the same and its interests are little diversified. A few men, therefore, will possess all the knowledge needed for proper representation. Were the interests and affairs of each individual State perfectly simple and uniform, knowledge of them in one part would imply knowledge of them in every other, and the whole State might be competently represented by a single member taken from any part of it. Comparing the different States together, we find a great dissimilarity in their laws, and in many other circumstances connected with the objects of federal legislation, with all of which the federal representatives ought to have some acquaintance. While a few representatives from each State, then, may bring with them due knowledge of their own State, every representative will have much information to acquire concerning all the other States. The changes of time, as remarked before, on the comparative situation of the different States, will have an assimilating effect. The effect of time on the internal affairs of the States, taken singly, will be just the contrary. At present, some of the States are little more than a society of farmers. Few of them have made much progress in those branches of industry that give variety and complexity to the affairs of a nation. These, however, will in all of them be the fruits of a more advanced population, and will require, on the part of each State, a fuller representation. The foresight of the convention has accordingly taken care that the progress of population may be accompanied with a proper increase in the representative branch of the government.

The experience of Great Britain, which presents to mankind so many political lessons of both warning and example, and which has been frequently consulted in these inquiries, corroborates the result of the reflections we have just made. The number of inhabitants in the two kingdoms of England and Scotland cannot be put at less than eight million. The representatives of these eight million in the House of Commons number five hundred and fifty-eight. Of this number, one-ninth are elected by three hundred and sixty-four persons, and one-half by five thousand seven hundred and twenty-three persons. It cannot be supposed that the half thus elected, and who do not even reside among the people at large, can add anything either to the security of the people against the government or to the knowledge of their circumstances and interests in the legislative councils. On the contrary, it is notorious that they are more frequently the representatives and instruments of the executive magistrate than the guardians and advocates of popular rights. They might therefore, with great propriety, be considered as something more than a mere deduction from the real representatives of the nation. We will, however, consider them in this light alone. We will not extend the deduction to a considerable number of others who do not reside among their constituents, are very faintly connected with them, and have very little particular knowledge of their affairs. With all these concessions, only two hundred and seventy-nine persons will be the depository of the safety, interest, and happiness of eight million. That is to say, there will be one representative only to maintain the rights and explain the situation of TWENTY-EIGHT THOUSAND SIX HUNDRED AND SEVENTY constituents, in an assembly exposed to the whole force of executive influence and extending its authority to every object of legislation within a nation whose affairs are in the highest degree diversified and complicated. Yet it is very certain not only that a valuable portion of freedom has been preserved under all these circumstances, but that the defects in the British code are chargeable, in a very small proportion, on the legislature's ignorance of the people's circumstances. Allowing this case the weight due to it, and comparing it with that of the House of Representatives as explained above, it seems to give the fullest assurance that a representative for every THIRTY THOUSAND INHABITANTS will render the latter both a safe and competent guardian of the interests committed to it.
